extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, artists, and students of aesthetics interested in crafting sublime and beautiful effects
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic principles for sublime and beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies 18th‑century aesthetic criteria for producing the sublime and the beautiful in art, sensation, and language — e.g., how darkness, size, smoothness, variation, color, taste, and words produce terror or delight. Useful for creative writers and artists aiming to evoke these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darkness as a cause of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness can be a source of the sublime because, in utter darkness, we cannot know our degree of safety; we are ignorant of surrounding objects and potential dangers, producing terror and awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use darkness to induce terror/astonishment by exploiting uncertainty about safety and the unknown — e.g., inability to know where to defend oneself, fear of stumbling or falling. The effect is general and may be innate to mankind, not merely due to local superstitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association vs. innate terror (darkness and supernatural imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness may be linked with ghosts and goblins by association, but it is more plausible that darkness, being naturally terrifying, was chosen as the fitting scene for such representations rather than the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using supernatural associations, consider whether the terror comes from learned association (nurse/old woman teaching a child) or from a broader, possibly innate, effect of darkness; both can be used but have different persuasions. For narrative design, associations amplify pre-existing fear in darkness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackness as partial darkness and source of uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackness (a more confined idea than darkness) can produce uneasiness or horror even without associative causes, as illustrated by the blind boy struck with horror on first seeing black objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat black elements in imagery as capable of producing immediate discomfort or horror; black as 'vacant spaces' among colors causes sudden relaxation/convulsion in the eye and mind. Use contrasts with surrounding colors to heighten the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/physiological effects of darkness (ocular strain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme darkness may physically affect the eye (pupil/iris tension and spasms), producing painful sensations and luminous flashes — bodily effects that then influence the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting darkness, consider physiological consequences (strain, flashes, startle responses) to ground psychological terror in bodily sensation. Small embodied details (eye strain, startle upon sudden darkness) increase verisimilitude of fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackness causes convulsive response through sudden relaxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Black areas amid surrounding color create a sudden relaxation of ocular tension followed by a convulsive recovery — analogous to unexpected changes that startle the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt contrasts (a black patch among colors, sudden cessation of sound or light) to exploit sensory convulsions: the unexpected change produces violent starts, awakening, or shocks. Avoid predictable repetition that diminishes this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of blackness moderated by custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Although black/ darkness may be originally painful, custom reconciles us to them and their sterner effects are softened by gloss, smoothness, or agreeable incidents; but original impression remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated exposure or aesthetic softening (gloss, pleasant context) reduces terror; writers can moderate black/ dark imagery with texture, shine, or pleasant associations to prevent overwhelming horror when undesired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty grounded in bodily relaxation (physical cause of love)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects act by relaxing the body's fibres; signs include reclining head, partially closed eyelids, slow breath, soft sighs, languor, and composed posture. Relaxation underlies positive pleasure and the passion of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke beauty/attraction, depict physical relaxation and languor in observers and subjects. Compose scenes that produce gentle bodily yielding (soft posture, slow breathing) to induce sympathetic relaxation in readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness as a principal cause of visual beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness, a primary source of tactile pleasure, is transferable to visual beauty: smooth bodies relax the senses and are universally associated with pleasing effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize smooth textures, surfaces, and transitions in description to elicit pleasure. In visual imagery, suggest surfaces that cause 'gentle' stimulation rather than jagged or angular forms which rouse tension or pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness (taste) as analogue of smoothness and source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweet tastes are the 'smooth' of taste; they are relaxing and pleasurable, often rooted in early life experiences (milk, sweet fruit) and composed of smooth vehicles (water/oil) plus a relaxing salt (sugar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing taste in description, use sweetness to suggest relaxation, comfort, and original pleasantness (childhood nourishment). Contrast sweet/smooth tastes with pungent/rough tastes to signal strengthening or bracing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness relaxes across senses (cross-modal principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smooth/sweet qualities across touch, taste, smell, and hearing relax the system (e.g., sweet smells induce drowsiness); languages often link 'soft' and 'sweet' linguistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage cross-sensory analogies (sweet/smooth smell, touch, sight) to compound the effect of beauty. Employ multisensory smoothness to deepen the reader's bodily relaxation and pleasurable response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation (gentle, continual, insensible) as central to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects exhibit continual, insensible variation in the direction of parts — never long uniform, never abruptly varied; gentle oscillation (rising and falling) relaxes more than absolute rest or violent change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rhythm, line, and motion in prose or description to vary gently and continuously. Avoid monotony (unchanging repetition) and avoid sudden harsh angles or jerks which produce tension rather than pleasure. Use moderate, repeated variation (rocking, gradual undulation) to soothe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale: smallness often enhances beauty, greatness tends to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Smallness as such is compatible (and often enhancing) of beauty; extraordinary largeness tends toward terror and the sublime, which can overpower qualities of beauty. Very small size only fails when perceived as monstrous or disproportionate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scale deliberately: use modest, delicate scale for affection and love; reserve very large scale and vastness when aiming for awe, terror, or the sublime. Be mindful of cultural associations of giants/huge size with tyranny and horror; dwarfishness can be grotesque if proportions are coarse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and transparency produce pleasure when even and smooth
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent bodies that transmit and reflect light evenly (softened transmitted light and even reflection of the proper color) are pleasing; muddy, interrupted rays (opaque particles) make a color disagreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual description, favor clarity, transparency, and even color presentation. Avoid 'muddy' or uneven color images unless the aim is discomfort. Shape and presentation (gradual, judicious variation) heighten the pleasurable effects of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of word types and their emotional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Words operate differently from natural objects; Burke divides words into aggregate words (stand for composed natural objects), simple abstract words (stand for single simple ideas), and compound abstract words (arbitrary unions standing for general concepts). Compound abstracts do not raise precise ideas but act as sounds that, by repeated use in emotional contexts, produce similar effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing, choose word types deliberately: compound abstract words (virtue, honor) work by association and habit rather than by evoking clear sensual images; to move passions directly, prefer concrete, aggregate, or simple abstract terms that tie to sensory impressions or situational occasions. Use the habitual emotional uses of abstract words to your advantage but be aware they often lack precise imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: General words taught before particular ideas shape disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Most general moral words (good, evil, virtue, vice) are learned before particular actions they denote, and thereby instill love or abhorrence by early emotional training rather than by precise conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ general moral language carefully: early or repeated exposure to general evaluative words can predispose readers' judgments without supplying concrete reasons. For persuasive writing, supplement general terms with illustrative particulars to avoid empty rhetoric.
